A longueur is a stretch or passage within a book, film, play, speech, or piece of music that feels tediously slow and dull — a section that drags on, loses your attention, and makes you feel like time is crawling. Think of it as a "dead spot" inside an otherwise larger work.

The key idea is that it doesn't describe the entire work as boring. It describes a specific section or period within something that, as a whole, might even be quite good.
What Makes It Different From Just Saying "Boring"?

This is important. Saying "the movie was boring" means the whole thing failed to hold your interest. But spotting a longueur is a more precise and surgical judgment — it means:

"This particular section dragged. It slowed things down unnecessarily. It made me restless and impatient. And it didn't need to be this long."

A seasoned film critic, for instance, might say: "The film is largely magnificent, but it suffers from longueurs in the second act." That tells you something very specific and useful — the film isn't bad overall, but there are particular stretches where it loses its energy and your attention starts to wander.

A longueur is not just about something taking a long time. It's about something feeling longer than it should — the dragging, restless feeling where you're glancing at the clock, flipping pages impatiently, or shifting in your seat. It's the subjective experience of time slowing down because the content isn't earning your attention.

This is a subtle but crucial point: a three-hour film can have zero longueurs if every scene crackles with energy. A thirty-minute speech can have painful longueurs if the speaker meanders, repeats themselves, or pads their points with unnecessary detail.
Where You'll See This Word Used

Longueur is almost exclusively used in critical or intellectual writing — book reviews, film criticism, literary essays, opera reviews, and cultural commentary. It's a word critics reach for when they want to say, with precision and elegance, that a work loses its momentum in places. You are far more likely to read it than to hear it in everyday conversation.

You will almost always see this word in the plural form: longueurs. This is because creative works rarely have just one problem patch — they tend to have several. So the typical usage sounds like:

  • "The novel has its longueurs, but the final hundred pages are extraordinary."
  • "Despite some longueurs in the middle section, the symphony builds to a breathtaking conclusion."

The singular longueur is valid but rarer, and you'd use it when pointing to one specific dragging moment:

  • "The trial scene is the one major longueur in an otherwise taut thriller."

1. "I loved the documentary, though there were a few longueurs whenever it shifted away from its central subject."
  2. "Even Shakespeare's greatest plays have longueurs that modern audiences find hard to sit through."
  3. "The speech was passionate, but the longueurs in the middle lost the crowd's attention."
A longueur is a tediously slow, dragging passage within a larger work — a section that outstays its welcome, saps your attention, and makes time feel heavier than it should.
